title: ⭐⭐ Practice: wishes, family ties and the present perfect

questions.prompt: This sentence is wrong: "Rania has met her Nan at the station yesterday." Which correction makes it right?

options.text: Rania has met her Nan at the station since yesterday.
Rania has meet her Nan at the station yesterday.
Rania is meeting her Nan at the station yesterday.
Rania met her Nan at the station yesterday.

questions.explanation: "Rania met her Nan at the station yesterday." is the correction: yesterday names a moment that is over, and only the past simple can stand next to it. "Rania has met her Nan at the station since yesterday." keeps the present perfect and adds a starting point, but meeting somebody at a station happens once and does not go on from yesterday until now; "Rania has meet her Nan at the station yesterday." leaves the verb in its base form where the past participle met is compulsory; and "Rania is meeting her Nan at the station yesterday." describes something in progress, which yesterday makes impossible.

questions.prompt: Hedi's mother died when he was six, and his father married again three years later. What does Hedi call his father's new wife in English?

options.text: his mother-in-law
his stepmother
his grandmother
his stepdaughter

questions.explanation: "his stepmother" is right: the wife of your father, when she is not your own mother, is your stepmother — stepmum in everyday speech. "his mother-in-law" names the mother of your husband or of your wife, a link that does not exist here; "his grandmother" is the mother of one of your parents; and "his stepdaughter" names the relation in the other direction, and for a girl — Hedi is his stepmother's stepson.

questions.prompt: Nizar had one ticket left for Saturday's match. He gave it to his little brother and stayed at home. Which adjective from the lesson describes him?

options.text: arrogant
proud
selfish
kind

questions.explanation: "kind" is right: giving up something you wanted for yourself so that somebody else can enjoy it is exactly what kind describes. "selfish" is its opposite, since a selfish brother keeps the ticket; "arrogant" describes somebody who believes he is better than the people around him, which Nizar never shows here; and "proud" names the good opinion you have of yourself or of somebody close to you, not the act of giving something away.

questions.prompt: Sami asks Firas: "Have you ever been to Tozeur?" Firas went there with his class last spring. Which reply is correct English?

options.text: Yes, I have. I went there with my class.
Yes, I have been there with my class last spring.
Yes, I am been there with my class last spring.
Yes, I have go there with my class last spring.

questions.explanation: "Yes, I have. I went there with my class." is right: a question with ever is a present perfect question, so the short answer repeats have, and the speaker switches to the past simple as soon as he gives the moment. "Yes, I have been there with my class last spring." keeps the present perfect beside last spring, a finished moment that forbids it; "Yes, I am been there with my class last spring." replaces the auxiliary have with am; and "Yes, I have go there with my class last spring." leaves the verb in its base form where a past participle is compulsory after have.

questions.prompt: Put these words in the right order to make one correct sentence: since / phoned / her / not / March / she / has / Nan.

options.text: Has she not phoned her Nan since March.
She not has phoned her Nan since March.
She has not phoned her Nan since March.
She has not phoned since March her Nan.

questions.explanation: "She has not phoned her Nan since March." is the right order: in a negative present perfect the pieces come in one fixed sequence — subject, then has, then not, then the past participle, then the person you phoned, and only at the end the time marker. "She not has phoned her Nan since March." puts not in front of the auxiliary, but not always comes after it. "Has she not phoned her Nan since March." uses the word order of a question to make a statement. And "She has not phoned since March her Nan." pushes the person after the time marker, which English never does when the object is that short.

questions.prompt: Read this note Yosra pinned on the family board: "I started my nursing course in October. I have not missed a single lesson since then. I passed my first test last month, and I have already chosen the hospital where I want to work." Which statement is true?

options.text: Yosra has missed one or two lessons since October.
Yosra has not missed a lesson since her course started.
Yosra still does not know which hospital she wants.
Yosra passed her first test before her course started in October.

questions.explanation: "Yosra has not missed a lesson since her course started." is right: the note says she has not missed a single lesson since then, and then refers to October, when the course began. "Yosra has missed one or two lessons since October." contradicts that negative sentence; "Yosra still does not know which hospital she wants." ignores I have already chosen, where already says the choice is made; and "Yosra passed her first test before her course started in October." puts the test before the course, although the note dates it last month, well after October.
